claims.text: What the Glean Blueprint Consultation is, why it exists, its three steps, and the outcomes it produces for customers, partners, and Glean
claims.checked_by: Workbook author attribution; not independently re-verified by the studio

claims.text: Most enterprises have already experimented with AI. Many have run assistants, chatbots, or internal pilots. Far fewer can point to a result their finance team accepts: more revenue, lower cost, or lower risk for a specific part of the business. That gap is why the Blueprint Consultation exists.
claims.checked_by: Studio author: drafted from the cited source text; no verbatim excerpt recorded; SME verification pending

claims.text: The Glean playbook describes the market plainly: the time of experimentation is ending. Buyers increasingly expect a new AI investment to prove the return they were promised, not just impress in a demo. "Pilot purgatory" is the failure mode you are trying to avoid: a long trial with no agreed success measure, no executive owner, and no decision at the end. The Blueprint Consultation lets the account team partner with the customer early, before anyone discusses a pilot. Together you find the strongest use cases and work out how to show their value quickly.

claims.text: The Blueprint Consultation is a structured series of customer conversations. The goal is to move to a pilot only when one is truly needed. The playbook frames three jobs for the process: Cut through ambiguity. Anchor each use case to a business outcome, prioritize by impact and effort, set clear success metrics, and confirm executive sponsorship with mutual action plan checkpoints. Validate value fast. claims.text: It is not a free pilot, a general product tour, or an open-ended brainstorm. A compelling demo is not a validated business case. The deliverable is a decision-ready plan: prioritized workflows, an evidence-labeled value case, and an agreed way to validate. It is never a promise of guaranteed savings. In plain language "We will agree the outcomes that matter to you, look at how the work happens today, and bring leadership an evidence-labeled value case and a recommendation for how to validate it."

claims.text: Business impact should connect to cost, revenue, or risk, because those are what executive sponsors fund. The Glean Value Playbook puts it directly: time saved is an input, not an outcome. The outcome is what happens with the time: revenue influenced, costs avoided, risks reduced, capacity redeployed, or quality improved. Compare two statements. "Save 30 minutes a day" is an activity claim. "Cut RFP response time so the team can answer more RFPs each quarter" is a value story, because it names a business result and a way to measure it.
